newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan considers beefing up securities watchdog.
newsitem.headline: Japan considers beefing up securities watchdog.

text.p: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) said on Monday that it was considering increasing staff at Japan's securities watchdog and imposing harsher penalties for illegal securities deals, following a recent scandal involving Nomura Securities.

These issues will be discussed by the Securities and Exchange Council, an advisory panel to the finance minister, and may be included in set of recommendations the panel is due to issue by June, a MOF official said.

The council is currently discussing ways to implement Japan's "Big Bang" financial reform plan and issues relating to the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), and harsher penalties for illegal deals would be among items to be considered by the panel, he said.

Nomura faces potentially stiff penalties over a scandal in which two of its directors made apparently illegal deals and funnelled funds to a corporate client linked by Japanese media to a former "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.
The scandal has also led some to question whether the SESC, which is investigating the case, and other authorities are equal to the task of policing the industry.
The SESC, which is under the supervision of the finance minister, was set up in 1992 after a scandal in which many brokers improperly covered favoured clients' investment losses.
Another MOF official said the number of staff members at the SESC is too small at 89, compared with about 2,700 at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
The securities watchdog has been keen to increase its staff in order to ensure the fairness and transparency of the securities market, financial sources said.

In order for Japan to achieve the proposed liberalisation of its financial markets by 2001, it must improve and strengthen the SESC's investigative resources by boosting its workforce and budget, the sources said.

The watchdog lacks the right to take punitive action itself but can recommend that the finance minister mete out administrative punishment and can ask prosecutors to take legal action against possible criminal violations.
Penalties under Japan's securities law are decided by the courts after prosecutors make an indictment.
